claims.text: Targeted colonic delivery of propionate via inulin-propionate ester (10 g/day for 24 weeks) significantly reduced weight gain compared to control in overweight adults.
Oral sodium butyrate administration (4 g daily for 4 weeks) improved peripheral and hepatic insulin sensitivity in healthy lean men, but not in men with metabolic syndrome.
Rectal infusion of 180 mmol acetate increased serum glucagon levels by approximately 26% and decreased free fatty acid levels by 22% in healthy human adults.
Resistant starch supplementation (30 g/day for 4 weeks) improved whole-body insulin sensitivity by approximately 13% in healthy adults.

evidence.description: In a 24-week trial by Chambers et al. (2015), only 4% of participants receiving 10 g/day inulin-propionate ester gained 3% or more body weight, compared to 25% in the control group.

Hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp measurements by Bouter et al. (2018) showed significant improvement in peripheral and hepatic insulin sensitivity in lean participants following 4 weeks of 4 g/day oral sodium butyrate.
Wolever et al. (1991) measured a ~26% increase in serum glucagon and a ~22% decrease in free fatty acid levels after acute 180 mmol rectal acetate infusion.
Robertson et al. (2005) observed a ~13% increase in whole-body insulin sensitivity via euglycemic-hyperinsulinemic clamp after 4 weeks of 30 g/day resistant starch supplementation.

methodologies.name: Systematic narrative literature review
methodologies.description: Literature search executed in PubMed and SCOPUS using specific SCFA search strings combined with topic keywords to synthesize human, animal, and in vitro evidence on SCFA and health.
conditions: In vitro and ex vivo colonic models

limitations.text: Human intervention studies examining the effects of SCFA on gut permeability, mucosal immunity, and metabolic parameters are limited in number, duration, and sample size.
Faecal SCFA concentrations reflect only distal colonic excretion and fail to accurately represent in vivo production or absorption kinetics across proximal colonic sites.
Mechanistic findings from animal studies frequently rely on administration routes (e.g., intragastric or colonic infusions) that do not directly translate to oral dietary intakes in human physiology.

future_work.text: Conduct well-controlled, longer-term human SCFA intervention studies measuring SCFA fluxes and kinetics using stable isotope techniques.
Investigate heterogeneity in metabolic response to SCFA interventions based on baseline metabolic phenotype, dietary fibre type, and colonic fermentation site.
Control for confounding variables in human microbiome interventions, including diet, physical activity, medication use, and gut transit time.
